parts:
Hello !

I have been using the code below to fit a random intercepts (variance components) model.

data {
    int<lower=1> n2 ; 
    int<lower=1> N ;
    real y[N] ;
    int school[N] ;
}
parameters {
    real u2_z[n2] ;
    real<lower=.1,upper=100> sigma ;
    real<lower=.1,upper=100> sigma_u2;
    real <lower=0,upper=1000> beta;
}
model {
    real mu[N];
    for (i in 1:N)
      mu[i] <- beta + u2_z[school[i]] * sigma_u2;

    y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
    u2_z ~ normal(0, 1) ;
}

This would be fitted in lme4 as
lmer(outcome ~1 + (1|school.ID),data=dt.all)

I now want to include a term for random slope, which would be fitted in lme4 as

lmer(outcome ~1 + (year|school.ID),data=dt.all)
or
lmer(outcome ~1 + (year-1|school.ID),data=dt.all)

The variable year is a factor with 3 levels., Please can anyone help me modify the stan model to implement these ?

Thanks  !
JK

> The variable year is a factor with 3 levels., Please can anyone help me modify the stan model to implement these ?

You just need to add another term to mu[i]
for the slope * predictor.

Assuming the predictor is x[i], the loop's just:

for (i in 1:N) {
real intercept;
real slope;
intercept <- beta + u2_z[school[i]] * sigma_u2;
slope <- gamma + v2_z[school[i]] * sigma_v2;
mu[i] <- intercept + slope * x[i];
}

And you can use the same implicit and explicit priors
for gamma, v2_z and sigma_v2 as you used for beta, u2_z
and sigma_u2 (assuming you also want to restrict gamma to
be positive).

You've already applied what we've taken to calling the "Matt trick"
(after Matt Hoffman, who also invented NUTS) to your code, which perhaps
makes it a little harder to see what's going on (but much more efficient
to sample from). If you instead wrote your model as:

intercept ~ normal(beta,sigma_u2);
y ~ normal(intercept[school[i]],sigma);

it should be clearer that the slope + intercept model is:

intercept ~ normal(beta,sigma_u2);
slope ~ normal(gamma,sigma_v2);
y ~ normal(intercept[school[i]] + slope[school[i]] * x[i], sigma);

Ideally, Stan would figure out the transforms on its own,
but not yet.

- Bob

>

Stan just has a base reader class from which a model
reads data.

In the command-line code, it's implemented
with a dump reader (which doesn't yet handle all the
creative variation in R's dump() output).

In RStan, it's implemented in RStan to read from
an R object. So that'd be the place to look for
what's going on with the types.

I'm guessing the following intended behavior may have
something to do with it:

The model will issue calls to read integer arrays
(for integer arrays in a Stan model) or double arrays
(for everything else). If the input is integers, it
should still be readable as a double by casting.

That's what the dump() reader implementation does and
is what the RStan implementation should do.

- Bob

I now use the "Multivariate Matt Trick" (also mentioned by Terrance) where quantities that have a multivariate normal distribution under the theoretical model are in practice, expressed as a function of standard normals and a Cholesky factor. See

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Drawing_values_from_the_distribution

  real mu[N];
  int k;
  matrix[n2,N_year] slopes_error;
  slopes_error <- slopes_z * transpose(cholesky_decompose(Tau)) ;
for (i in 1:N) {

k <- year[i];

                       tau[k] * slopes_error[school[i],k]);

On 10/23/12 4:32 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> OK, now I have a question (forgive me if the answer's already in the manual). Suppose I define a parameter theta to
> have a normal (mu, sigma) distribution but then theta is declared as real<lower=0, upper=0.5>. Does Stan then work with
> the truncated normal density (i.e., getting the correct normalizing factor which is now a function of mu and sigma) or
> does it just use the normal density without adjusting for the truncation?

First, you never get the full normalization term in Stan.
All constant terms are dropped. In the normal, we never
include the constant normalizing term -log(sqrt(2*pi)).

The difference between

x ~ normal(mu,sigma); // no space before '('!!!

and

x ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[0,0.5];

is that the latter applies the truncated density and
the former does not.

If the variable x is declared as real<lower=0,upper=0.5>,
that is, with fixed bounds, then the first is OK as
we only need the density up to a proportion. If the
bounds were variable, you'd need the second form.

Assuming the bounds are properly declared for x,
we should be able to implicitly drop the truncation
in the future, but the code doesn't do that yet (it also
doesn't check ranges for x and return -inf if x is not
in the specified bounds and it probably should).

- Bob

First, you never get the full normalization term in Stan.
All constant terms are dropped.  In the normal, we never
include the constant normalizing term -log(sqrt(2*pi)).

The difference between

    x ~ normal(mu,sigma);   // no space before '('!!!

is that the latter applies the truncated density and
the former does not.

If the variable x is declared as real<lower=0,upper=0.5>,
that is, with fixed bounds, then the first is OK as
we only need the density up to a proportion.  If the
bounds were variable, you'd need the second form.
